posts.title: Ten minutes at the inkstone
posts.excerpt: Why every lesson begins by grinding ink, even though bottled ink exists.
posts.content:
New students always ask why we do not simply pour ink from a bottle. The answer is the ten minutes: grinding is when the shoulders drop and the breath slows.

Grind in small circles, with only a few drops of water at a time. When the stick drags a little and the ink holds a line on the stone, it is ready.

posts.title: Choosing a first brush
posts.excerpt: Goat hair, medium length, and why the cheapest brush in the shop is a false saving.
posts.content:
A first brush should be soft enough to forgive and long enough to show pressure. Goat hair does both.

Avoid brushes glued stiff for display. Soak the tip open slowly in lukewarm water before the first lesson.

posts.title: A hundred sheets a term
posts.excerpt: How much paper a student really uses, and which sheets to keep.
posts.content:
Most students write about a hundred practice sheets each term. Keep the best one from every lesson; by the end of the year the folder shows the progress better than any comment.

Store the paper flat and away from the window. Damp hanshi blots; very dry hanshi cracks the stroke.

posts.title: The seal comes last
posts.excerpt: A small red mark at the end of a composition, and when students earn their own.
posts.content:
In the kana and composition class students carve or order a small seal. It is pressed once, low on the sheet, after the last line is dry.

The seal is small on purpose. If it is the first thing you notice, it is in the wrong place.

posts.title: Saturday mornings with young learners
posts.excerpt: Big brushes, big paper and a cup of barley tea in the middle.
posts.content:
The Saturday class has nine students between seven and twelve. They write large, simple characters and are encouraged to make mistakes boldly.

Parents may watch from the veranda. Most of them, after a few weeks, ask about the adult evening class.

posts.title: The veranda exhibition
posts.excerpt: One week in late November when the students’ best sheets hang over the moss garden.
posts.content:
Each student chooses one sheet from the year. Tomo mounts them on plain card and hangs them along the veranda.

The gate stays open all week. Neighbours come in, sit for a while and leave without a word, which is the best review a calligrapher can receive.
